{{Short description|Mathematical theorem in complex analysis}}
[[File:Gösta_Mittag-Leffler_x_Brauer.jpg|thumb|Portrait of Gösta Mittag-Leffler]]
In [[complex analysis]], '''Mittag-Leffler's theorem''' concerns the existence of [[meromorphic function]]s with prescribed [[pole (complex analysis)|pole]]s. Conversely, it can be used to express any meromorphic function as a sum of [[Partial fractions in complex analysis|partial fractions]]. It is sister to the [[Weierstrass factorization theorem]], which asserts existence of [[holomorphic function]]s with prescribed [[Zero (complex analysis)|zeros]].

The theorem is named after the Swedish mathematician [[Gösta Mittag-Leffler]] who published versions of the theorem in 1876 and 1884.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Mittag-Leffler |date=1876 |title=En metod att analytiskt framställa en funktion af rational karakter, hvilken blir oändlig alltid och endast uti vissa föreskrifna oändlighetspunkter, hvilkas konstanter äro på förhand angifna |journal=Öfversigt af Kongliga Vetenskaps-Akademiens förhandlingar Stockholm |volume=33 |issue=6 |pages=3–16}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Mittag-Leffler |date=1884 |title=Sur la représentation analytique des fonctions monogènes uniformes dʼune variable indépendante |journal=Acta Mathematica |volume=4 |pages=1–79|doi=10.1007/BF02418410 |s2cid=124051413 |doi-access=free |url=https://zenodo.org/records/1751831/files/article.pdf }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Turner |first=Laura E. |date=2013-02-01 |title=The Mittag-Leffler Theorem: The origin, evolution, and reception of a mathematical result, 1876–1884 |journal=Historia Mathematica |language=en |volume=40 |issue=1 |pages=36–83 |doi=10.1016/j.hm.2012.10.002 |issn=0315-0860|doi-access=free |url=https://summit.sfu.ca/_flysystem/fedora/sfu_migrate/8209/etd3098.pdf }}</ref>

==Theorem==
Let <math>U</math> be an [[open set]] in <math>\mathbb C</math> and <math>E \subset U</math> be a subset whose [[limit point]]s, if any, occur on the [[Boundary (topology)|boundary]] of <math>U</math>. For each <math>a</math> in <math> E</math>, let <math>p_a(z)</math> be a polynomial in <math>1/(z-a)</math> without constant coefficient, i.e. of the form
<math display="block">p_a(z) = \sum_{n=1}^{N_a} \frac{c_{a,n}}{(z-a)^n}.</math>
Then there exists a [[meromorphic]] function <math>f</math> on <math>U</math> whose [[Pole (complex analysis)|poles]] are precisely the elements of <math> E</math> and such that for each such pole <math>a \in E</math>, the function <math>f(z)-p_a(z)</math> has only a [[removable singularity]] at <math>a</math>; in particular, the [[principal part]] of <math>f</math> at <math>a</math> is <math>p_a(z)</math>.  Furthermore, any other meromorphic function <math>g</math> on <math>U</math> with these properties can be obtained as  <math>g=f+h</math>, where <math>h</math> is an arbitrary [[Holomorphic function|holomorphic]] function on <math>U</math>.
(Here, note that a function being analytic and holomorphic are equivalent attributes)
===Proof sketch===
One possible proof outline is as follows. If <math> E </math> is finite, it suffices to take <math display="inline"> f(z) = \sum_{a \in E} p_a(z)</math>. If <math>E</math> is not finite, consider the finite sum <math display="inline"> S_F(z) = \sum_{a \in F} p_a(z)</math> where <math> F </math> is a finite subset of <math>E</math>. While the <math>S_F(z)</math> may not converge as ''F'' approaches ''E'', one may subtract well-chosen [[rational function|rational functions]] with poles outside of <math>U</math> (provided by [[Runge's theorem]]) without changing the principal parts of the <math>S_F(z)</math> and in such a way that convergence is guaranteed.

==Example==

Suppose that we desire a meromorphic function with simple poles of [[residue (complex analysis)|residue]] 1 at all positive integers. With notation as above, letting 
<math display="block">p_k(z) = \frac{1}{z-k}</math> 
and <math>E = \mathbb{Z}^+</math>, Mittag-Leffler's theorem asserts the existence of a meromorphic function <math>f</math> with principal part <math> p_k(z) </math> at <math>z=k</math> for each positive integer <math> k</math>. More constructively we can let 
<math display="block">f(z) = z\sum_{k=1}^\infty \frac{1}{k(z-k)} . </math>

This series [[Normal convergence|converges normally]] on any [[Compact space|compact]] subset of <math> \mathbb{C} \smallsetminus \mathbb{Z}^+ </math> (as can be shown using the [[Weierstrass M-test|M-test]]) to a meromorphic function with the desired properties.

== Pole expansions of meromorphic functions ==
Here are some examples of pole expansions of meromorphic functions:
<math display="block"> \pi\csc(\pi z)
= \sum_{n\in\Z} \frac{(-1)^n}{z-n}
= \frac1z + 2z\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{(-1)^n}{z^2 - n^2}</math>
<math display="block"> \pi\sec(\pi z)
= \sum_{n\in\Z} \frac{(-1)^{n-1}}{z-\left(n+\frac12\right)}
= 2\sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{(-1)^{n-1}(n+\frac12)}{z^2-(n+\frac12)^2}
</math>
<math display="block"> \pi\cot(\pi z)
= \lim_{N\to\infty}\sum_{n=-N}^N \frac1{z-n}
= \frac1z + 2z\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac1{z^2 - n^2}</math>
<math display="block"> \pi\tan(\pi z) = \lim_{N\to\infty}\sum_{n=-N}^N \frac{-1}{z-(n+\frac12)} = 2z\sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{-1}{z^2-(n+\frac12)^2} </math>
<math display="block"> (\pi\csc(\pi z))^2 = \sum_{n \in \Z} \frac1{(z-n)^2} </math>
<math display="block"> (\pi\sec(\pi z))^2 = \sum_{n \in \Z} \frac1{(z-(n+\frac12))^2}</math>
